articles.title: I built a self-hosted gig watcher so I stop refreshing job boards — it only pings me on new matches
articles.excerpt: Freelancers lose real money to latency. The best remote gigs get filled in the first few hours — the "Senior Backend Engineer, $120k, fully remote" posting is usually taken before you finish your seco…
articles.body: Freelancers lose real money to latency. The best remote gigs get filled in the first few hours — the "Senior Backend Engineer, $120k, fully remote" posting is usually taken before you finish your second coffee. So we all do the same embarrassing thing: keep 6 job boards open and refresh every 15–20 minutes, mostly seeing the same 300 stale listings. I got tired of it, so I built GigWatch — a small, self-hosted watcher that monitors live job/gig feeds, filters them against your skills, remembers what it has already shown you, and pings you (console, email, or Slack) only when a new matching gig actually appears . No dashboard to babysit. No account to sign up for. Just a process on a machine you already run.

articles.title: What actually happens in the 60 seconds after a buyer pays for your digital download (and the 7 days after)
articles.excerpt: A digital download sale looks instant from the seller's side: a notification, a payout pending, done. From the buyer's side it is a chain of about a dozen handoffs — payment, confirmation, email, link…
articles.body: A digital download sale looks instant from the seller's side: a notification, a payout pending, done. From the buyer's side it is a chain of about a dozen handoffs — payment, confirmation, email, link, file, first open — and every handoff is a place a sale can quietly break. This is that chain, annotated: what happens at each timestamp, what can go wrong there, and the fix to have ready before it does. T+0 seconds — the payment The buyer clicks pay. Their card is charged by your payment processor, and the processor — not your delivery tool — decides whether the money is good. That ordering matters: a well-built delivery flow waits for the processor's confirmation before it sends anything.

articles.title: The 4 rules in my CLAUDE.md that fixed most of my bad Claude Code sessions
articles.excerpt: Claude Code is amazing for about a week. Then it refactors a file you didn't ask it to touch, over-engineers a five-line fix, or proudly announces "done" for something that doesn't work. I use it dail…
articles.body: Claude Code is amazing for about a week. Then it refactors a file you didn't ask it to touch, over-engineers a five-line fix, or proudly announces "done" for something that doesn't work. I use it daily on client projects, and almost every one of those moments traced back to a single idea: The agent only knows what's in its context window right now. Not what it "learned" yesterday. Not your team's conventions. If it isn't in the context, it doesn't exist. So the job isn't "prompting" - it's deciding what goes into the context and what stays out. The cheapest, highest-impact place to start is your global ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md . Here are the four rules I put there. Rule 1 - Think before coding No silent assumptions. State what you're assuming. Surface tradeoffs. Ask before guessing.

articles.title: Malformed Metrics Query Response JSON — Rollback-Safe Worker Input Validation
articles.excerpt: Reject a malformed metrics query response before its JSON can influence paging or rollback. TL;DR: parse the body once, validate the exact fields used by the decision, preserve a bounded diagnostic re…
articles.body: Reject a malformed metrics query response before its JSON can influence paging or rollback. TL;DR: parse the body once, validate the exact fields used by the decision, preserve a bounded diagnostic record, and turn invalid input into an unknown evaluation rather than healthy or failed . For a nightly structured-log pipeline, that distinction keeps a broken monitoring response from approving a bad run or waking someone for data that never existed. The deciding constraint is rollback safety. A basic JSON.parse() plus optional chaining looks compact, but it merges transport success, JSON syntax, response shape, and query meaning into one optimistic path. The experiment here uses a stricter boundary: malformed or incomplete evidence cannot vote.

articles.title: I built an MCP server that lets AI agents investigate videos
articles.excerpt: Hey DEV! First post here 👋 I've been working on an open-source project called Urma, a local MCP server that lets AI hosts retrieve captions and frames from videos. I recently shipped its first stable…
articles.body: Hey DEV! First post here 👋 I've been working on an open-source project called Urma , a local MCP server that lets AI hosts retrieve captions and frames from videos. I recently shipped its first stable release, so I thought I'd introduce it here. The idea is quite simple. Let's say you're asking an AI agent to research how a particular feature works. It searches the documentation, goes through a few GitHub issues (including one closed in 2021 with no explanation), and eventually finds a recording where someone demonstrates the feature. That recording could be a 40-minute conference talk, with the relevant part buried somewhere around minute 37. Naturally. An agent with web access can find the recording itself.

articles.title: Earth's poles shifted surprisingly fast during the age of dinosaurs, ancient sea levels reveal
articles.excerpt: The location of Earth's geographic poles has changed several times over the past 320 million years in a process known as true polar wander.
articles.body: The location of Earth's geographic poles has changed several times over the past 320 million years in a process known as true polar wander, according to measurements of ancient flooding brought about by sea level changes resulting from our planet's crust shifting relative to Earth's spin axis. Such a shift can affect climate, both on local scales and globally, as regions that were by the poles find themselves moving down to lower latitudes and vice versa. This can then affect atmospheric circulation patterns, which affect climate across the world. The changes would have affected the environments in which life developed and evolved, from the age of the dinosaurs through to some of our oldest primate ancestors.

articles.excerpt: Tesla has stopped taking orders for the Model 3 Premium in Canada, the Shanghai-built trim that brought the electric sedan down to $39,490 CAD. The automaker says it has used up its import quota for C…
articles.body: Tesla has stopped taking orders for the Model 3 Premium in Canada, the Shanghai-built trim that brought the electric sedan down to $39,490 CAD. The automaker says it has used up its import quota for Chinese-made EVs and doesn’t expect to reopen orders until March 2027. But the Canadian government’s own tracker tells a different story: 33,069 of the 49,000 permits for China-made EVs in the current quota year are still available. more…
